assumptions: The only parameters are an arbitrary natural n and an arbitrary real function f on PrimitiveBasis(n+1).
There is no normalization, nonzero, positivity, boundedness, or sign assumption on f. The real expression under each square root is nonnegative because it is a sum of squares.
definitions_and_conventions: PrimitiveBasis k is the set of functions from Fin k to Fin 2: its elements have k ordered coordinates, each taking the value zero or one.
Fin.snoc b d extends b by placing d in the last coordinate, indexed by n; this marginal combines amplitudes differing in that last coordinate.
pairNorm(a,b) is the nonnegative real square root of a squared plus b squared. The marginal is a real amplitude function, rather than a function returning the squared marginal weights.
normSq(h) is the finite sum of the real squares of h over its complete bitstring carrier. No square root is taken in normSq itself.
edge_cases: For n=0, PrimitiveBasis 0 contains exactly the empty bitstring, so the left side has one summand and the right side has the two one-bit summands.
Every PrimitiveBasis n has 2^n elements and is nonempty, even at n=0; the outer norm sums are therefore never empty.

If both amplitudes in a pair are zero, the corresponding marginal amplitude is zero. The all-zero function is admitted. Negative real amplitudes are admitted and their signs are discarded by this marginal.
limits: The proposition is an exact real algebraic identity for squared norms. It does not assert a circuit, a state-preparation algorithm, a measurement procedure, a gate count, query complexity, runtime, or finite-precision error bound.

It does not recover the individual amplitudes or their signs from the marginal, and it does not state a complex-amplitude or phase-preservation result. Normalized input would imply normalized marginal, but normalization is not a premise of this target.
The supplied definitions suffice to reconstruct this statement; their noncomputable annotations alone establish neither an executable algorithm nor an inefficiency result.
reconstruction.reconstructed_statement: For every natural number n, including zero, and every real-valued function f on the set of bitstrings of length n+1, define a real-valued function g on bitstrings b of length n by g(b) = sqrt(f(b followed by 0)^2 + f(b followed by 1)^2). Then the sum, over all length-n bitstrings b, of g(b)^2 equals the sum, over all length-(n+1) bitstrings x, of f(x)^2. Thus the specified operation of replacing each pair of amplitudes sharing the first n coordinates by its nonnegative Euclidean length preserves the total squared Euclidean norm exactly.

assumptions: f is an arbitrary real table on n+1 wires; no positivity or normalization is assumed
the marginal is defined by the sibling-pair Euclidean length as in the source
conventions: normSq g is the sum of squared entries; wires are little-endian with the last bit split off by snoc
pairNorm is the nonnegative Euclidean length of a pair
source_question.question: For a finite real amplitude table f on n+1 wires, define its low-wire marginal by taking, at each prefix word b, the Euclidean length of the sibling pair (f at b-with-last-bit-0, f at b-with-last-bit-1). Prove that the total squared Euclidean norm of the marginal equals the total squared Euclidean norm of f. Explain why this makes the recursive marginal pass norm-faithful.
source_question.reference_answer: Write normSq g = sum over basis words of g^2, and for a prefix word b let m(b) = pairNorm(f(snoc b 0), f(snoc b 1)) with pairNorm(a,b) = sqrt(a^2+b^2). First, pairNorm squares cleanly: pairNorm(a,b)^2 = a^2 + b^2, because pairNorm is the square root of the nonnegative quantity a^2+b^2 and squaring a square root of a nonnegative real returns the radicand. Hence m(b)^2 = f(snoc b 0)^2 + f(snoc b 1)^2 for every prefix b. Summing over all prefix words b: normSq(marginal f) = sum_b m(b)^2 = sum_b [ f(snoc b 0)^2 + f(snoc b 1)^2 ]. Now use the bijection between words on n+1 wires and (prefix word b, last bit v) given by w = snoc b v, which partitions every full word uniquely by its last bit. Reindexing the full sum normSq f = sum over w of f(w)^2 along this bijection and splitting the last bit into the two cases v=0 and v=1 gives exactly sum_b [ f(snoc b 0)^2 + f(snoc b 1)^2 ]. The two expressions coincide, so normSq(marginal f) = normSq f. Norm-faithfulness follows: the recursive loader first prepares the marginal on the lower wires and then splits each marginal entry with one rotation; because each marginal step reproduces the exact squared norm, the induction hypothesis about the normalized lower state transfers without any loss or rescaling, which is precisely the invariant the first-column proof consumes.

rubric.criterion: Establishes pairNorm(a,b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 (square of a square root of a nonnegative radicand), hence m(b)^2 = f(snoc b 0)^2 + f(snoc b 1)^2.
Uses the (prefix word, last bit) bijection w = snoc b v to reindex the full squared-norm sum.
Splits the last-bit sum into v=0 and v=1 to match the marginal sum, concluding normSq(marginal f) = normSq f.
Explains that exact squared-norm preservation per level is what carries the normalization invariant through the recursion.

formal_context.target: ∀ {N : ℕ} (A : _root_.Matrix (Fin N) (Fin N) ℝ) (i j : Fin N), i ≠ j → ∀ theta : ℝ, (QuantumBlockEncoding.AdjacentGivens.rotateRows A i j theta).det = A.det

assumptions: N is any natural number; A is any real square matrix of that size; i and j are valid row indices; the sole substantive hypothesis is i != j; theta is any real number.
There is no invertibility, orthogonality, normalization, sparsity, nonzero-determinant, or restriction on the angle.
definitions_and_conventions: A has row and column carrier Fin N and real entries. The ambient rotateRows definition also supports rectangular matrices, but this target specializes it to square matrices so that its determinant is defined.

Both replacement rows use entries from the original A. For every column, the ordered pair of entries in rows i and j is multiplied on the left by the real two-by-two matrix with first row (cos(theta/2), -sin(theta/2)) and second row (sin(theta/2), cos(theta/2)).

The rotation angle in that two-dimensional plane is theta/2, not theta. Its orientation is fixed by the negative sine in the new row i and positive sine in the new row j, using the ordered pair (i,j).

The definition tests row=i first and row=j second. The hypothesis that the indices differ ensures these two branches describe separate rows. The target imposes neither adjacency nor a numerical ordering on i and j.
edge_cases: For N=0 there are no row indices, so there is no instance with chosen i and j. For N=1 indices exist but the distinctness hypothesis cannot hold. These sizes impose no nonvacuous determinant identity for a distinct row pair.
Singular A is included; both determinants are then zero. Theta=0 is included and gives the original matrix.

Coincident indices are excluded. At i=j, the first branch of the ambient definition takes priority and would scale that row by cos(theta/2)-sin(theta/2); the target supplies no determinant-preservation claim for that case.
limits: The conclusion is determinant preservation by one specified row operation. It does not assert an elimination algorithm, that an entry is zeroed, a method for choosing theta, a factorization into rotations, or any gate or runtime bound.

The import or namespace name supplies no adjacency assumption and no additional circuit semantics. The target does not itself state norm preservation, matrix unitarity, or a quantum-gate implementation.
The supplied formula fixes the half-angle, row order, and signs without requiring additional definitions.
reconstruction.reconstructed_statement: For every natural number N, every real N-by-N matrix A, every ordered pair of row indices i and j in Fin N with i different from j, and every real number theta, form a new matrix by replacing row i with cos(theta/2) times the old row i minus sin(theta/2) times the old row j, replacing row j with sin(theta/2) times the old row i plus cos(theta/2) times the old row j, and leaving every other row unchanged. The determinant of the resulting matrix equals the determinant of A exactly.

assumptions: Finite-dimensional real square matrix; two distinct selected rows
Determinant is multilinear and alternating in rows
conventions: RY half-angle convention for the rotation coefficients
A single row transposition contributes sign -1
Original derivation from inspected local source; no fresh Lean verification
source_question.question: Replacing two distinct rows i and j of a square matrix by the linear mixtures (a*row_i + b*row_j) and (c*row_i + d*row_j) multiplies the determinant by (a*d - b*c). Use this to prove that a plane rotation acting on rows i and j by the half-angle convention leaves the determinant unchanged.
source_question.reference_answer: Expanding the determinant linearly in the two updated rows produces four terms. The two terms that reuse the same original row twice (coefficients a*c on row_i in both slots, and b*d on row_j in both slots) are determinants with two equal rows, hence 0. The surviving cross terms are a*d times the original determinant and b*c times the determinant with rows i and j swapped; the swap introduces one transposition, so its sign is -1 and that determinant equals -det. Collecting gives (a*d)*det + (b*c)*(-det) = (a*d - b*c)*det. For a plane rotation the mixing coefficients are a=cos(t/2), b=-sin(t/2), c=sin(t/2), d=cos(t/2), so a*d - b*c = cos^2(t/2) + sin^2(t/2) = 1. Therefore the rotation preserves the determinant exactly. This is an exact algebraic identity about the determinant, not an arithmetic evaluation cost.

rubric.criterion: Kill the repeated-row terms via equal-row determinant 0
Identify the swap term sign as -1 and assemble a*d - b*c
Specialize rotation coefficients to get factor cos^2+sin^2=1

formal_context.target: ∀ {l r : ℕ} (A : QuantumBlockEncoding.TensorTrainCanonical.Core l r), A * A.transpose = 1 → (QuantumBlockEncoding.TensorTrainCanonical.complexCore A).conjTranspose * QuantumBlockEncoding.TensorTrainCanonical.complexCore A = 1

assumptions: l and r are arbitrary natural numbers and A has real entries with the stated carriers.

The sole algebraic hypothesis is A*A.transpose = I_l, namely pairwise orthonormality of all rows. No square shape, nonempty dimension, additional normalization, or separate dimension inequality is explicitly assumed.
In finite dimensions the row-orthonormality hypothesis can hold only when l <= 2*r, but that inequality is a consequence or feasibility constraint rather than an additional binder in the target.
definitions_and_conventions: Core(l,r) is literally a real matrix with row carrier Fin l and column carrier the Cartesian product Fin 2 times Fin r. The first output component b is a two-valued index and the second q ranges over r values.

complexCore is the transpose of A followed entrywise by the canonical real-to-complex embedding: it reverses the row and column carriers. It does not merely cast A while retaining its original orientation.

The hypothesis uses an ordinary real transpose. The conclusion uses the complex conjugate transpose of B. Because every entry of B is embedded from a real number, conjugation leaves those entries unchanged.

Both displayed identity matrices have row and column carrier Fin l. In components, the hypothesis says that for every a,a' in Fin l, the sum over b in Fin 2 and q in Fin r of A(a,(b,q)) times A(a',(b,q)) equals one when a=a' and zero otherwise. The conclusion says the corresponding complex inner products of columns of B have exactly those values.
The product carrier specifies the two output components explicitly; the packet supplies no separate flattening into Fin(2*r), bit-endianness convention, or requirement that r be a power of two.
edge_cases: When l=0, A has no rows and B has no columns. Both the hypothesis and conclusion concern the unique zero-by-zero matrix and hold vacuously for every r, including r=0.

When r=0 and l>0, the column carrier of A and row carrier of B are empty. A*A.transpose is the zero l-by-l matrix, so the identity hypothesis cannot hold. The conditional target therefore has no such nonvacuous instance.

Rectangular cases with 0<l<2*r are permitted. Their conclusion is an isometric embedding and does not require B to be surjective. When l=2*r the carriers have equal cardinality, but the target still explicitly states only B's left Gram identity.
limits: The target proves the conditional identity B.conjTranspose*B = I_l for this already supplied A. It does not construct a row-orthonormal core, a tensor-train canonicalization algorithm, or a decomposition of an arbitrary tensor.
It does not generally conclude B*B.conjTranspose equals the identity on the output carrier; that would be full unitarity and need not hold for rectangular B.

It does not specify a unitary extension, ancillas, a preparation circuit, successive core contractions, gate counts, computational complexity, or approximation and finite-precision bounds. The output dimension 2*r alone is not an encoding of all output degrees of freedom into a specified number of qubits.
The ambient definitions suffice to determine the exact real-to-complex conversion and orientation. No original source wording or proof was needed or inspected.
reconstruction.reconstructed_statement: For every pair of natural numbers l and r and every real matrix A whose rows are indexed by Fin l and whose columns are indexed by Fin 2 times Fin r, suppose A times its ordinary transpose equals the identity matrix on Fin l. Define the complex matrix B with rows indexed by Fin 2 times Fin r and columns indexed by Fin l by B((b,q),a) equal to the real entry A(a,(b,q)), embedded in the complex numbers. Then B's conjugate transpose times B equals the identity matrix on Fin l. Equivalently, real orthonormal rows of the l-by-(2r) matrix A become complex orthonormal columns of the (2r)-by-l matrix B, so the complex linear map B from complex l-space to complex (2r)-space is an isometry.

assumptions: A is a real core with orthonormal rows A * A^T = 1
the complex embedding uses (bit, new bond) as output rows and old bond as input columns
conventions: conjTranspose is the complex conjugate transpose; realness means entrywise conjugation is the identity
the isometry condition is (complexCore A)^dagger (complexCore A) = 1 on the input-bond index
source_question.question: A real tensor-train core carries orthonormal rows (its row-canonical condition). Show that embedding such a core into a complex matrix with the physical bit and new bond as output rows and the old bond as input columns yields a genuine circuit isometry: the conjugate-transpose times the matrix is the identity on the input-bond index. Explain why real orthonormal rows translate exactly to orthonormal complex input columns under this orientation.
source_question.reference_answer: Let A be a real core with A * A^T = 1 (orthonormal rows). The complex embedding places (bit, new bond) as the output row index and the old bond a as the input column, with entry the real number A_{a,(bit,newbond)} viewed as a complex number. The isometry claim is (complexCore A)^dagger * (complexCore A) = 1 on the old-bond index. Fix input columns a and c; the (a,c) entry of the product is sum over all outputs (bit, newbond) of conj(entry at output,(a)) times entry at output,(c). Because every entry is a real number embedded in the complex field, its conjugate is itself, so this equals the real sum over outputs of A_{a,out} * A_{c,out}, which is precisely the (a,c) entry of A * A^T. By hypothesis A * A^T = 1, so the sum is 1 when a = c and 0 otherwise. Splitting the complex equality into real and imaginary parts: the real part reproduces the (a,c) entry of A * A^T (equal to the Kronecker delta), and the imaginary part vanishes because every summand is a product of reals and hence has zero imaginary component. Therefore (complexCore A)^dagger (complexCore A) is the identity. The conceptual point: the row-canonical condition on the real core, summation over the physical bit together with the new bond, is literally the Gram matrix of the complex input-bond columns under this output-row/input-column orientation; realness makes conjugation trivial so the real orthonormality transfers verbatim to complex column orthonormality.

rubric.criterion: States the isometry target (complexCore A)^dagger (complexCore A) = 1 and expands the (a,c) entry as a sum over outputs (bit, new bond) of conj times entry.
Uses realness of the entries (conjugate = itself) to reduce the sum to the real sum A_{a,out} A_{c,out}, i.e. the (a,c) entry of A * A^T.
Invokes A * A^T = 1 to get the Kronecker delta, splitting the complex identity into a real part (= delta) and a vanishing imaginary part.
Explains the orientation point: real orthonormal rows are exactly the Gram matrix of complex input-bond columns, so orthonormality transfers verbatim.
